question: A credit-limit feature serves consumers in Brazil, Portugal and Colorado. Which obligation group appears in all three markets?
options: AI-generated content labeling
Rights around automated decisions: LGPD Art. 20 review, GDPR Art. 22 safeguards (and AI Act high-risk duties later), and Colorado's notices and consumer rights for consequential decisions
Algorithm filing with a national regulator
Nothing: credit is only regulated by banks
explanation: Automated decisions about credit trigger rights in every one of those markets, with different instruments and dates. One review path with recorded criteria serves all of them.

question: Why does the map evaluate status on a date passed in, instead of always using today?
options: Dates make the code faster
The same table must answer what applies today, at launch and at future deadlines such as December 2027
Laws never change, so the date is irrelevant
Bills need a date to become law
explanation: Planning needs the future view. An obligation that is upcoming at today's date may already apply on your launch date.

question: How should a bill such as Brazil's PL 2338/2023 appear in the map?
options: As an obligation that applies today
Not at all
As a proposed watch item with its source, kept separate from laws and reviewed every quarter
As a prohibition
explanation: Bills are worth watching and designing toward, but they create no obligation until enacted.

question: The rules table was last reviewed 140 days ago. What should the map do?
options: Nothing, since laws rarely change
Flag the table as stale so a review happens before anyone relies on it
Delete the table
Mark every obligation as proposed
explanation: AI law moved several times in 2025–2026. A dated table with a freshness check makes staleness visible instead of silently trusted.

question: Which pattern shows up in the EU, California, China and South Korea alike?
options: A ban on all chatbots
Transparency for AI interaction and AI-generated content (disclosure and labeling)
Mandatory open-sourcing of models
A single global regulator
explanation: Disclosure and labeling duties recur across very different regulatory styles, which is why provenance and disclosure controls are worth building once.
